notes: The encyclopaedia's articles on how the game works (game/encyclopaedia.py). Each: id, title, group, text (paragraphs, blank-line separated). Keys named as the game's own (rebound keys show under Settings > Controls).

articles.title: Getting to orbit
articles.text:
An orbit is falling round a body fast enough sideways to keep missing it. Low Earth orbit needs about 7.8 km/s sideways; a rocket climbs out of the thick air first, then turns over and builds that speed.

The gravity turn: a little after lift-off tip the nose about 10 degrees east (W) and switch stability assist to prograde (F). Gravity bends the climb over by itself. East, because the Earth's turning gives you some 400 m/s for free at the equator.

Burn until the apoapsis (the highest point of the path) is above the air, cut the engines and coast up to it; there, burn prograde until the periapsis is up too. The map's Maneuver panel plans that burn: Circularize.

articles.title: Staging
articles.text:
A rocket throws away what it no longer needs: empty tanks and their engines are dead weight. Space fires the next stage: the first lights the engines, later ones fire decouplers (dropping a stage) and light the next engines, arm parachutes.

The HUD shows the stage, how many are left, and the propellant in the stage burning. A stage run dry: Space. Delta-v (the speed change left in the tanks) is in the HUD's propulsion column.

articles.title: Stability assist
articles.text:
T turns stability assist on: the reaction wheels and the engines' gimbals hold the vessel steady. F cycles its mode: hold (where it points now), prograde (along its motion), retrograde (against it: for slowing down and landing), maneuver (along a planned burn).

W / S pitch, A / D yaw, Q / E roll by hand. Reaction wheels need power.

articles.title: Maneuver nodes
articles.text:
On the map (M) the Maneuver panel plans a burn: a node at the apoapsis, the periapsis or a few minutes on, or a suggested one (circularize, capture at another body, come down). Its handles set how much along prograde, normal (out of the orbit's plane) and radial; the dashed orbit shows what it makes.

The HUD counts down to the burn's start (half its length before the node) and shows the m/s left as you fly it. Stability assist's maneuver mode points along it. Warp slows on its own as it nears.

articles.title: Transfers and launch windows
articles.text:
To reach another body, leave when it is ahead of you by the right angle: a launch window. The map's Navigation panel, with a target chosen, finds the next window and the burn (a Lambert solution between the two orbits), and later a course correction.

Crossing into a body's sphere of influence, its gravity takes over; the patched conics on the map show the path through each. Arrive on a flyby, then burn retrograde at the periapsis to be captured (Maneuver: Capture).

articles.title: Time warp
articles.text:
. warps faster, , slower, / back to real time, in steps up to 10,000,000x. Under thrust or in the air it holds to 5x (the physics needs small steps). Coasting, vessels move on rails: along their conic, exactly.

Warp stops for a planned burn, a sphere of influence crossing, the flight computer's next command.

articles.title: The air, heating and parachutes
articles.text:
Every body with an atmosphere has its own: Earth's, Mars's thin carbon dioxide, Venus's crushing one, Titan's thick cold nitrogen. Drag slows you with the air's density and your speed squared; the HUD shows the pressure and temperature outside.

Coming in fast, the air ahead is squeezed and heats the hull: a heat shield takes it (keep it first: retrograde); other parts burn up past their limit. A shallower entry heats less but longer.

Parachutes are armed by staging and open low and slow enough; too fast, they tear. Unfolded solar wings tear off in fast air too.

articles.title: Landing
articles.text:
Without air, only the engine slows you. The HUD counts down to the landing burn (the latest moment a full-thrust burn stops you at the ground: BRAKE NOW); burn retrograde, then ease off to come down slowly.

A vessel stands if it comes down slow enough for its parts (a few m/s), upright, on ground no steeper than its feet hold. Landing legs (G) widen the stance: more slope, harder landings. The HUD shows the slope under you.

articles.title: Mars's weather
articles.text: Mars has seasons and dust storms (from the real calendar of its year): a storm thickens the dust, darkens the sky, cuts solar power and blows hard across the ground. The HUD shows the weather over a vessel low at Mars.

articles.title: Docking and RCS
articles.text:
Docking ports join two vessels into one. Target the other (Vessels list, L, or the map), close in on the RCS thrusters (arrows, H / N: they move without turning), and press B: the vessel lines its port up with the target's and comes in. Ports at the ends of stacks and side ports on radial groups.

Docked, propellant moves between tanks; the Vessels list undocks. Within 200 m and 2 m/s, propellant can move between vessels too (a depot).

articles.title: Power
articles.text:
Everything aboard draws power: avionics, life support, cameras, transmitters, reaction wheels turning hard. Batteries store it; solar wings (U unfolds them) make it in sunlight, less far from the Sun and none in shadow; RTGs and reactors make it anywhere.

Out of power, a vessel has no reaction wheels, no link, no flight computer and no science. The HUD's POWER shows the charge and the net; the part editor shows a design's budget.

articles.title: The link and light delay
articles.text:
Ground stations round the Earth (the Deep Space Network's) keep a probe in touch, if its antenna reaches and nothing is in the way. Commands go at the speed of light: seconds to the Moon, minutes to Mars, hours to the outer planets. A crewed vessel flies at once; a probe without a link cannot be flown at all.

The flight computer (C) runs a sequence of commands on its own (wait for an altitude, burn, stage, point retrograde...): written, checked and sent like any command.

articles.title: Propellants and boil-off
articles.text:
Engines burn their own propellant: kerosene and oxygen (RP-1/LOX), liquid hydrogen and oxygen (hydrolox: efficient, but it boils off), methane and oxygen (methalox), and storable hypergolics (they keep for years and light every time).

Cryogenic propellants boil away in sunlight unless insulated or cooled (a cryocooler, powered). ISRU plants make propellant from ice (hydrolox) or Mars's air (methalox).

articles.title: Orbital debris
articles.text: Stages left in orbit stay there, their orbits decaying in the thin top of the air; a collision makes a cloud of fragments that spreads round the orbit. The HUD warns of a close pass (a ping) with the time and the miss distance: a small burn moves you out of the way.

articles.title: Rovers and rotorcraft
articles.text:
On wheels, W / S drive and A / D steer, on power; steep or fast ground rolls a rover over. A rover carried on a lander is separated beside it, on the ground.

A rotorcraft lifts on its rotors in air (thin air, a big rotor and little mass: Mars's helicopter): the throttle sets the lift.

articles.title: Science
articles.text: Instruments aboard (R runs them) learn something new in each situation: on the ground or flying low or high over each region of each body, in space near it. Results are worth points recovered home, less transmitted. The science panel (K) shows what is left here; a survey camera maps a body, and the map shows its real detail where mapped.

articles.title: The space programme
articles.text:
In a career, every launch is paid for from the funds; a budget comes in on the first of each month, more with reputation. Missions on the real calendar (reach orbit, the Moon, sample return, the planets) pay funds and reputation; past a deadline, a mission fails and reputation falls. A recovered vessel pays back most of its cost.

Science points buy research (the tech tree): new parts. Astronauts are hired, fly, rest; they need supplies and take radiation far out.

articles.title: Reliability
articles.text: New engines and parts fail more often: every flight and ignition teaches the programme, and the record makes the next ones safer. A failure shows as a notice and on the HUD; the part editor shows each part's flight data.

articles.title: Saving
articles.text: Each game is saved as you play (every 30 s and on quitting), with a copy kept every 5 minutes and as something risky begins (a launch, a new sphere of influence, coming down to land): the title screen loads it. F5 quicksaves, F9 goes back to the quicksave. The pause menu's Revert goes back to the launch.
